title: Eight handfuls of grass
hookLine: a grass-cutter gives him grass; he makes a seat beneath the tree, facing east

lines: THE PLACE YOU SIT WHEN IT MATTERS.
WALKING TOWARD A GREAT FIG TREE.
cards: A chair at the kitchen table where the bills get paid. The edge of a bed where the hard phone calls get made. A back step for thinking.
Homes collect places like these without anyone deciding on them. Where a person sits can tell the body what's about to happen. It's late afternoon on the day of Sujata's milk-rice.
The wanderer is walking toward a great fig tree near the river. On the way, a man comes along the path carrying freshly cut grass. His name, the telling says, is Sotthiya.

teach.b: Sotthiya the grass-cutter sees the wanderer and, without being asked, offers him eight handfuls of grass. A small gift, the kind you'd give without thinking. The wanderer accepts it and carries it to the tree.
It's a fig, the kind called assattha, or pipal, with broad, heart-shaped leaves that tremble in the slightest breeze.
Soon it will have a new name: the Bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. Tradition holds that a descendant of it grows at that spot today, in Bodh Gaya, in India, where pilgrims come to sit beneath it.
The telling says he walks around the tree, looking for the right place. On the south side, the ground seems to tilt. He tries the west, then the north.

teach.h: ONLY THE EAST SIDE IS STEADY.
teach.b: Then he stands on the east side, and the earth feels steady. There. He spreads the grass on the ground and sits on it, cross-legged, his back to the trunk, facing east, toward where the sun will rise.
That's all that happens today. A man takes a gift of grass and makes a seat. But Buddhists keep telling this small moment because of what a seat means.
You can think about doing something forever.
The moment you sit down to do it, you've decided.
And the telling gives this seat a name of its own: the unconquered seat.

how: Pilgrims visit the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, in India, to sit and meditate beneath it, and some Buddhists keep a dedicated seat or cushion at home for daily practice.

o: the pipal fig that became the Bodhi tree
the banyan tree where Sujata made her vow
the soft grass he spread to make his seat

games.q: what's inside the seat — tap the pairs.
p: the pipal fig, later the Bodhi tree

s: the wanderer asked the grass-cutter for the grass
in the telling, Sotthiya offered it without being asked.
tradition holds that a descendant of the Bodhi tree grows at Bodh Gaya

he sat facing east, his back to the trunk.

games.q: you walk around the great tree, looking for a place to sit. on the south, west and north the ground feels unsteady. what do you do?
o: sit anyway on the north side.
games.why: on the east side the earth feels steady. he spreads the grass there and sits, facing the sunrise.

practice: Make a seat right where you are, a cushion, a folded blanket, a chair, the edge of the bed, arranged on purpose the way the wanderer spread his grass, facing east or toward the light if you can.
Sit down slowly, knowing you're sitting, and feel the seat take your weight: the backs of the legs, the sit bones, the feet on the floor, the spine rising easy and upright. Then just sit.

wordCard.voice: Assattha. The pipal fig tree where the wanderer spread a grass-cutter's gift of grass as his seat, facing east.

orig.note: Pali: the pipal fig tree (Ficus religiosa), later called the Bodhi tree.

carryVoice: Your line: a seat is a decision. Yours can be any chair at all. Fifty days now.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): Sotthiya's grass and the seat facing east
